steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on appearance-based eye gaze estimation for human-robot interaction, where we train a neural network on real images plus synthetic faces. Motivate gaze in HRI, explain why it is hard, and state our system and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. HRI and the need for robots to understand humans
2. Eye gaze as a social signal; difficulty; gaze vs. head pose
3. Our modular approach
4. RGB-only, position-independent system
5. Synthetic dataset contribution

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. HRI
- rapidly growing; manufacturing, healthcare, education, entertainment
- key aspect: robots understand/respond to human behavior and intentions
- recognizing human-specific signals -> humanized robots

2. Eye gaze
- key social signal: attention, interest, emotions
- accurate gaze estimation essential human-like ability for HRI
- approaches: model-based, appearance-based, hybrid
- hard: variability of gaze directions, head position, lighting in real settings
- head pose often used as proxy, much better observable
- but direct gaze = better communication cue and agent's spatial predictor, not fully substitutable
- eye tracking -> more efficient collaboration than head tracking (quantitative + subjective)

3. Modular approach
- reuse existing solutions: face detection, head pose estimation
- off-the-shelf components save time/effort, narrow focus
- our addition: NN module, cropped eyes -> 2D gaze (pitch and yaw)

4. System properties
- normal RGB camera only, no IR filters, no extra hardware
- works from different positions relative to head; robust to head positions

5. Synthetic dataset
- 57,375 faces, MetaHuman tool, 15 characters, controlled head pose and gaze
- significantly improved accuracy vs. only smaller real dataset (Columbia Gaze)

steps.text:
Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) is a field that is growing rapidly and has many applications in areas like manufacturing, healthcare, education, and entertainment. One of the most important parts of HRI is that robots need to be able to understand and respond to human behavior and intentions. Being able to recognize human-specific signals will make the robots humanized.

Eye gaze is a key signal that people use in social interactions to show their attention, interest, and emotions. So accurate gaze estimation is an essential human-like ability for robots, needed for successful HRI. Several approaches have been proposed for gaze estimation, including model-based, appearance-based, and hybrid methods. But accurate gaze estimation is still a challenging task, because gaze directions and head position vary a lot, and lighting conditions in real settings vary too. Because of this, head pose estimation has often been used as a proxy, since it is much better observable. However it has been argued that direct eye gaze estimation is a better communication cue and spatial predictor of the agent, and head pose estimation cannot completely substitute it. An eye tracking system has been shown to allow more efficient human-robot collaboration than a comparable head tracking approach, both in quantitative measures and in the subjective evaluation by the human participants.

- reuse existing solutions: face detection, head pose estimation
- off-the-shelf components save time/effort, narrow focus
- our addition: NN module, cropped eyes -> 2D gaze (pitch and yaw)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) is a field that is growing rapidly and has many applications in areas like manufacturing, healthcare, education, and entertainment. One of the most important parts of HRI is that robots need to be able to understand and respond to human behavior and intentions. Being able to recognize human-specific signals will make the robots humanized.

Eye gaze is a key signal that people use in social interactions to show their attention, interest, and emotions. So accurate gaze estimation is an essential human-like ability for robots, needed for successful HRI. Several approaches have been proposed for gaze estimation, including model-based, appearance-based, and hybrid methods. But accurate gaze estimation is still a challenging task, because gaze directions and head position vary a lot, and lighting conditions in real settings vary too. Because of this, head pose estimation has often been used as a proxy, since it is much better observable. However it has been argued that direct eye gaze estimation is a better communication cue and spatial predictor of the agent, and head pose estimation cannot completely substitute it. An eye tracking system has been shown to allow more efficient human-robot collaboration than a comparable head tracking approach, both in quantitative measures and in the subjective evaluation by the human participants.

In this paper we approach the problem of eye gaze estimation for HRI. We don't start from scratch, but instead we use existing recent solutions to concrete subproblems such as face detection or head pose estimation and build a modular system. Using existing off-the-shelf components saves time and effort, and it also lets us narrow down the focus to what is left in solving the problem. What we add to the system is the neural network module that maps the cropped eyes to 2D gaze information (pitch and yaw).

One main difference of this system from others is that it can work with only a normal RGB camera, without any special IR filters or any additional hardware. It also works from different positions relative to the head of the person whose eye gaze it is predicting, and it should work reliably even with different head positions.

The second contribution is a generated synthetic labeled dataset of 57,375 human faces, made with the MetaHuman tool using 15 characters, with controlled head pose and eye gaze directions. Using this data improved the accuracy of our model significantly compared to using only a smaller training dataset of real images (Columbia Gaze).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) is a rapidly growing field with numerous applications in areas such as manufacturing, healthcare, education, and entertainment [1]. One of the most important aspects of HRI is the ability of robots to understand and respond to human behavior and intentions [2]. Their ability to recognize human-specific signals will make the robots humanized [3].

Eye gaze is a key signal that people use in social interactions to convey their attention, interest, and emotions. Accurate gaze estimation by robots is therefore an essential human-like ability for successful HRI [4]. Several approaches have been proposed for gaze estimation, including model-based, appearance-based, and hybrid methods. However, due to the high variability of gaze directions and head position, as well as lighting conditions in real settings, accurate gaze estimation remains a challenging task. Head pose estimation, which is much better observable, has therefore often been used as a proxy. Nevertheless, it has been argued that direct eye gaze estimation is a better communication cue and spatial predictor of the agent, and cannot be completely substituted by head pose estimation. An eye tracking system has been shown to allow for more efficient human-robot collaboration than a comparable head tracking approach, according to both quantitative measures and subjective evaluation by the human participants [5].

In this paper, we approach the problem of eye gaze estimation for HRI not from scratch but by taking advantage of existing recent solutions to concrete subproblems such as face detection or head pose estimation, building a modular system. Using existing off-the-shelf components not only saves time and effort but also lets us narrow down the focus to what is left in solving the problem. In particular, what we add to the system is the neural network module that maps the cropped eyes to 2D gaze information (pitch and yaw).

One of the main differences of this system from others is its ability to work with only a normal RGB camera, without any special IR filters or additional hardware. It also works from different positions relative to the head of the person whose eye gaze it is predicting, and should work reliably despite different head positions.

The second contribution of our work is a generated synthetic labeled dataset of 57,375 human faces (using the MetaHuman tool) with 15 characters, with controlled head pose and eye gaze directions. Using this data significantly improved the accuracy of our model compared to only using a smaller training dataset of real images (Columbia Gaze).

References:
[1] H. Su, W. Qi, J. Chen, C. Yang, J. Sandoval, and M. Laribi, “Recent advancements in multimodal human–robot interaction,” Frontiers in Neurorobotics , 2023.
[2] A. Thomaz, G. Hoffman, and M. Cakmak, “Computational human-robot interaction,” New Foundations and Trends , vol. 4, no. 2-3, p. 105–223, 2013.
